Debt Crisis Strikes Saudi Real Estate Sector, Projects Stalled and Jobs at Risk

A sudden debt crisis is sending shockwaves through Saudi Arabia’s real estate industry, leaving major development sites idle and thousands of workers facing uncertainty. The crisis, triggered by a sharp rise in interest rates and tightening credit conditions, has forced numerous property firms to seek urgent restructuring as access to new financing has dried up.

In Riyadh and Jeddah, several high-profile residential and commercial projects have come to a standstill in recent days. Al Thimar Properties, one of the sector’s largest developers, announced late Wednesday that it had frozen work on its luxury towers in north Riyadh, citing “unprecedented funding challenges.” Other firms, including Najm Real Estate and Al Masaakin Holdings, have requested debt repayment extensions from creditors.

Industry analysts report that more than SAR 25 billion in loans are at risk of default if current conditions persist. “We are witnessing the most severe liquidity crunch the Saudi real estate market has faced in over a decade,” said Khalid Al-Zahrani, a real estate market analyst based in Dammam. “Developers are unable to roll over maturing debt, which is forcing them to halt ongoing projects and reconsider future investments.”

The Saudi Real Estate Union warned in a statement that as many as 40,000 industry jobs could be impacted if the crisis continues. “Our members are reporting widespread layoffs and furloughs, particularly among site workers and project managers,” said union spokesperson Reem Al-Fahad. “Many families depend on these wages, and the uncertainty is causing significant distress.”

On several construction sites in the capital, workers have been seen packing up equipment and leaving. Some have expressed concern about outstanding wages and the future of their employment. “We have not received clear information from our supervisors,” said one site worker, who declined to be named. “All we know is that work has stopped, and we have to wait.”

Government officials have stated they are monitoring the situation and are in talks with industry leaders, but no rescue package has yet been announced. The outlook for the sector remains uncertain as the debt crisis unfolds.
